templates.name: John Snow: The Broad Street pump
templates.hook: One map, one meeting, one handle.
whatMakesItWork: Snow's map, rebuilt from the data: All 578 deaths and 13 pumps from the digitized map. Press "Nearest pump" and 359 of them light up in Broad Street's patch.
The brewery puzzle: A ledger of who died and who didn't, with the water column hidden. Reveal it: beer and a private well, against two tubs of pump water.
An honest result chart: Scrub Snow's own table day by day. The handle came off on 8 September, after cases had already fallen from 143 a day to 12.
The skeptic as the reference: Whitehead's own words play from "a careful investigation would refute it" to the cesspool two feet eight inches from the well.

beats.job: State the outcome and the time it took, with two or three summary metrics.
Who they are in a few facts, so readers can check if they match; ask them.
The stakes in the customer's own terms and numbers, plainly.
The standard approach, done properly, and why it couldn't explain the problem.
What was done, by whom, in what order, with dates.
The one picture that makes the cause obvious.
The cases that should break the story and instead confirm it.
The customer's own data, gathered separately, pointing the same way.
The numbers before and after, including what the product did not cause.
Time, meetings, cost and effort, and how long adoption took.
A named quote that starts with doubt, next to the claim it supports.
If you're like them: three steps with owners and dates.

templates.name: Mr. Miyagi: Wax on, wax off
templates.hook: Four days of chores. Every one a block.
whatMakesItWork: The chores flip into blocks: Four cards (sponge, sandpaper, fence brush, house brush) turn over one by one into the block each one trained. Click to flip them back.
The deck quizzes you: A no-notes check with three questions and instant feedback, because tested students remembered 56% a week later and re-readers 42%.
The practice log ties the belt: Two weeks of spaced practice, each chore returning a little later each time; log the days and a gi belt fills to the knot.
Outcomes, not topics: "Block a punch without thinking about it", with how it gets checked. Karate history and belt theory are struck off the syllabus.

beats.job: Name the learner, the program and the first thing to bring.
Up to four things they will be able to do, each with how it gets checked.
The stakes in writing: what changes if they learn this, and what happens if they don't.
One skill, practiced on the slide, before the theory.
A no-notes quiz with instant feedback. Retrieval beats re-reading.
What builds on the first one, one new piece at a time.
Now name what they have been practicing and why it works.
A calendar where each skill returns after growing gaps, with unannounced checks.
Where it gets used for real, under pressure, with nobody prompting.
Who is in their corner, starting with an active manager.
Exactly what to do first, and when the first check-in is booked.

templates.template: Results report and letter to owners
templates.name: Berkshire Hathaway: The letter to shareholders
templates.hook: One number, one yardstick, and the mistakes left in.
whatMakesItWork: Scrub sixty-one years: Drag through every year of the real per-share table: the lines compound on a log scale, the gap strip turns gray in the 21 years Berkshire trailed, and 2025 is one of them.
A ledger of mistakes, priced: Nine confessions from the letters, from an eighth of a point in 1964 to Pilot, filtered by did, passed and waited, each with the cost the letters put on it.
Memo mode: The whole report as a one-page letter, opening "Dear Doris and Bertie". One click rewrites it as an earnings call, which is the argument for writing plainly.
Weather gets credit: Every line of the good year is marked earned or luck. A year with no U.S. hurricane landfall goes in the luck column.

beats.job: Lead with one result and the yardstick it is measured against, over the longest honest period.
Show every period against that yardstick, misses included, so the reader can check the claim.
Name the wins and sort each into earned or luck.
List the errors with dates and costs, in the first person, with what you took from each.
Rank where money (or effort) goes, and the test each use has to pass.
Restate the standing principles, including the ones that cost you.
Praise by name, criticize by category; tell one story that shows the culture.
Say plainly who now runs what, and what stays the same.
Write the whole report as one page for a smart reader outside your field.
Set expectations for next year, lower ones included, and say when you will report again.

templates.name: Coca-Cola: The Pepsi Challenge and New Coke
templates.modelName: the New Coke competitive analysis structure
templates.hook: 200,000 sips said change it. The can disagreed.
whatMakesItWork: Take the blind test: Pick cup M or cup Q on the one-sip promise, then see the reveal: you just voted like 191,000 tasters in Project Kansas.
Sip versus can: Behind a one-way mirror, toggle one sip, half a can, and a whole can, and watch the winner change from the sweeter formula to the one people grew up with.
The SWOT with an empty box: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats are all full. The fifth box, what customers feel, says "Not measured" until you press "What we missed".
The test plays out: The recommendation says "watch the hotline"; then the hotline counts from 400 to 1,500 calls a day and the timeline runs 79 days to Classic.

beats.job: The finding and the matchup in one line: who is winning what.
The one question this analysis answers, and the decision riding on it.
Share over time for you and the main rival, with the gap you are trying to explain.
A grid of the dimensions that matter, with the one row you lose highlighted.
What buyers say they want, and exactly how you measured it: sample, cost, format.
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, plus a box for what customers feel, so it leads to a move.

beats.beat: What the data can't tell us
beats.job: The limits of the method: what it measured versus how people actually buy and use.
Three things that must now be true, and the stake if you act on them.
The move, the date, and the signals with baselines that would prove you wrong.
The lesson to carry into the next analysis, stated as a rule.

templates.name: NASA: The 1975 Graphics Standards Manual
templates.hook: One agency. One mark. No exceptions.
whatMakesItWork: Clear space you can break: Drag the center name toward the mark: the three-stroke-width zone turns red the moment you cross it, and grows with every decal size.
Nine misuses, flippable: Outlined, shadowed, squashed, sideways, and rule two, "such as a circle". Flip each tile between wrong and right.
The red, tested on every ground: Pantone 179 with its hex, RGB and process values, then click five backgrounds to see which colors the mark may wear on each.
The forms finally arrive: The 1975 manual promised new forms "at a later date". Here is one, with a grid overlay you can switch on.

beats.job: Name the standard and its promise: one brand, applied one way.
Show the cost of inconsistency: every team drawing the brand its own way.
What the logo is, how it is built, and the one rule: never redraw it.
The minimum air around the mark and the approved sizes, measured from the mark itself.
Exact values for every medium, and which color goes on which background.
The typefaces, the weights, and how names lock up with the mark.
The understructure every layout hangs from, shown on a real application.
The brand at its largest and smallest: vehicles, signs, forms, decals, with sizes.
The specific don'ts, drawn, so nobody has to guess.
Who owns the standard, and where each common question gets answered.
Close on what the standard protects over time.

templates.name: Hans Rosling: 200 countries, 200 years
templates.hook: Press play on 200 years.
whatMakesItWork: You take the chimp test: Three questions in the spirit of Factfulness, scored live against the 2017 public (9%, 13%, 37% right) and against chimps guessing at random (33%).
The chart actually plays: 184 countries from 1800 to 2025 on Gapminder's open data, with a play button, a year scrubber, live captions, and a number for every bubble you hover.
Sweden is the clock: Sweden's whole road on the chart, with South Korea, China, the USA, India or Nigeria laid beside it, then every country pinned to the year Sweden lived as long.
The dips get names: Click the outliers: the 1918 flu, China's famine, the Khmer Rouge, HIV in Botswana. Every one recovered.

beats.job: Name the dataset and the promise: what the one chart will show.
Draw the picture the audience already holds, so the data has something to overwrite.
Three quick questions that prove the misconception, scored against chance.
Explain the axes and ask the one question the chart answers.
Play the data over time; let people scrub, pause and hover.
Stop the clock on the surprise and put one number on it.
Follow a single case the audience knows, against one they don't.
Name the exceptions and what explains them, instead of averaging them away.
Turn the chart into one sentence the audience can repeat.
Three habits to take home, and a way to replay the chart.

templates.name: The Panama Canal: Sanitation first, then dig
templates.modelName: the Panama Canal project kickoff structure
templates.hook: The dig stays locked until the mosquitoes sign off.
whatMakesItWork: The dig is locked: A phase plan where "Dig at full scale" stays padlocked until Sanitation and Railway both sign off. Reset it and try to start digging early.
The French ledger becomes rules: Five crossed-out entries from 1881 to 1889, each one clicked open into what happened and the rule it gave us.
Havana is the proof: Gorgas's own monthly table: 310 yellow fever deaths in 1900, 18 in 1901 once the mosquito work began. Toggle the years and watch the bars fall.
Hindsight on the risk register: Flip from the 1905 plan to what happened. Four risks held. One assumption failed, and the deck says so plainly.

beats.job: The project and its one rule of order, in five words.
Answer first: the situation as it stands and the change you are making.
The last attempt's record, each failure turned into a rule.
One checkable outcome, plus the conditions that make it count.
What is in, and what is out for now, with the reason for each out.
Proof the approach has worked somewhere else, as a chart.
Phases with owners and gates; later phases stay locked until earlier ones sign off.
A RACI with exactly one accountable name per row.
Each risk with an owner and a fix; list the assumptions you have not tested.
How often you report, to whom, and status colors with fixed meanings.
Dated first moves and the one decision you need, with a named decider.

templates.name: Sherlock Holmes: The Baskerville case report
templates.hook: There is no curse. There was a cousin with a dog.
whatMakesItWork: The answer comes first: Holmes saved the solution for the fireside in the last chapter. The 2026 report opens on it: no curse, one cousin, one painted dog, case closed.
The evidence board has real string: Nine clues from the novel pinned to three findings. Click a finding and its strings light up: the boots, the cigar ash, the portrait.
The staffing plan has a twist: A map of the moor from Merripit House to the Grimpen Mire. Flip "As briefed" to "As run" and Holmes leaves London for a stone hut.
The curse gets an alibi: Curse, convict, butler, clergyman, typist: each suspect is struck through and stamped as its evidence lands.

beats.job: The engagement, the client, and the verdict in one line.
The answer first, three supporting points that don't overlap, and the status.
Situation, complication, and the question the client asked, in their words.
The method and where the work happened, staffing as run rather than as sold.
Every key piece of evidence linked to the finding it supports.
A full-sentence headline and the one exhibit that proves it.
One finding per slide, with a diagram the client can check for themselves.
The finding the client least wants to hear, with the number behind it.
The hypotheses you eliminated and the evidence that eliminated each one.
Actions with one owner and a date each; the most important one first.
What stays open, including what went wrong on your side.
Dates for what happens next and exactly what you need from the client.

templates.name: Julia Child: The French Chef
templates.hook: Live, one take, and the potato hits the stove.
whatMakesItWork: The agenda runs like a broadcast clock: A studio clock sweeps all 28 minutes in about fourteen seconds, the ON AIR light glows, and each segment lights up as the hand reaches it. Click a segment to jump.
You can overcrowd the pan: Drag the slider past eight pieces of beef and the copper sear turns to grey steam. The demonstration proves the one rule of a good stew.
A mishap button, with a playbook: Cause a mishap (the flipped potato, the burned-down studio, the crackling mic) and a calm three-step recovery plays, followed by what the show really did.
The poll answers back: Vote on what keeps you out of the kitchen and the reply appears on air. The live tally is one vote, and it is yours.

beats.job: Name the session and the one thing people will be able to do by the end.
Say how it runs: live or recorded, how long, and how to ask questions.
One credential the audience can check, plus why this person in particular.
Four to six segments with real timecodes, so people know when the good part is.
Do the thing on screen and let the audience change one variable.
The common mistake, what happens, and how to recover without stopping.
A poll or question at the halfway mark, answered on air.
The moves in the order people will use them, not the agenda again.
How the recording will reach the people who watch later.
One dated next session and the one resource to use tonight.

templates.name: Brownie Wise: The Tupperware party
templates.hook: Take it off the shelf. Throw it a party.
whatMakesItWork: Burp the seal yourself: Press the button and a drawn bowl does the whole demo: lid down, edge up, pfft, airtight. That one move is why stores couldn't sell it.
Shelf versus living room: Toggle the same 39-cent bowl between Aisle 6 and a party table ringed with ten coffee cups, and watch who shows the seal, who's watching, and what happens next.
One dealer compounds: Drag parties a week, guests, bookings and recruits, and watch one dealer become a sales force in three years, next to the real 20,000 by 1954.
The risk nobody listed: Plastic, the seal, and Jubilee prizes sinking into the Florida swamp are all handled. The last row is the founder, and it says plainly what happened in 1958.

beats.job: Name the product and the channel you are betting on, in one line.
What it is, what it costs, and the exact reason it isn't selling yet.
Show the product in today's channel next to the proposed one, and what changes.
Who buys, what they doubt, and where they already gather.
The sale step by step, ending in the step that starts the next sale.
Conversion at every step as a calculator, with the assumptions visible and adjustable.
Who pays what, and what each person in the chain earns.

templates.hook: The public first, whatever it costs.

whatMakesItWork: The budget always wins: Drag food, vet and toys as high as you like. The dog lands under therapy every time, because Leo's allowance quietly absorbs the rest.
